newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela calls Botha hard line on past provocative.
newsitem.headline: Mandela calls Botha hard line on past provocative.

text.p: President Nelson Mandela said on Friday he regretted the uncompromising stance of former President P.W. Botha and urged him to go before South Africa's "truth commission" to explain crimes committed under his apartheid era rule.
"It is regrettable that he has made a statement of that nature," South Africa's first black president told reporters in the Indian Ocean port city of Durban.

"His (Botha's) duty is to go to the TRC (Truth and Reconciliation Commission) and give his own version of what happened, because as things stand the evidence seem to point to him having committed some of the gross violations which we are complaining about," he added.
Botha said after two hours of talks with "truth commission" chairman Archbishop Desmond Tutu in the Cape on Thursday that he had nothing to apologise or seek amnesty for.

"I am not guilty of any deed for which I should apologise or ask for amnesty. I therefore have no intention of doing this," the 80-year-old ex-president said in a statement after talks with Tutu to seek his cooperation in uncovering the past.
Mandela said Botha was an old man, no longer well, who might expect to be honoured as a former statesman. But he added:

"When he makes a statement which is regarded by the majority of the country as being provocative and which might lead to the conclusion that he has no interest in the lives of hundreds of people who died as a result of gross human right violations, people may not appreciate whatever service he may have given."
Botha has been implicated in the planning of a violent 1980s government campaign against anti-apartheid groups aligned to Mandela's then-banned African National Congress (ANC).

Former police chief Johan van der Merwe said in an amnesty application last month that he was instructed to blow up the Johannesburg headquarters of the South African Council of Churches harbouring anti-apartheid groups in 1988.
He said the instruction came from Law and Order Minister Adriaan Vlok, who told him the order came directly from Botha.

Tutu's commission has until the end of 1997 to unravel the human rights record of the war over apartheid, to pardon human rights offenders on both sides of the struggle and to award limited compensation to victims.

Tutu, who has subpoenaed reluctant police, army and cabinet leaders of the apartheid era to appear before his statutory commission agreed to see Botha in his retirement town of Wilderness on Thursday.
Arguing against black demands that Botha should answer in public for the actions of his government, Tutu said he should be accorded the respect of a former head of state.
